resources.string: Explore the beauty of mathematics through interactive visualizations.
Visualize N-pointed regular stars drawn in one stroke.
Explore the most famous fractal. Zoom in to find infinite complexity.
Watch a hypotrochoid draw itself. Change the ring, wheel, and pen to close new curves.
Fix c and iterate z → z² + c from every point. Change c to grow new shapes.
Congratulations! You made a %1$d-pointed star in one stroke!
It is not possible to draw a %1$d-pointed star in one stroke.
Moving 1 dot at a time joins every neighbour in turn, so you get a regular %1$d-sided polygon rather than a star. Move 2 or more dots at a time to make a star.
Because %1$d is a prime you can actually choose any movement number and still get a %1$d-pointed star.

It is possible to draw %2$d different %1$d-pointed stars in one stroke. Mirrored stars are not counted. For example, moving 2 or 3 points at the same time to get a 5-pointed start is the same solution.

With %1$d dots available, moving %2$d dots at a time results in a %3$d-pointed star.

This tiny app renders an N-pointed regular star (if possible) using only straight lines without leaving the surface with the pen. The rules are that it starts in one point, and then draws straight lines always moving the same amount of dots at a time, until it comes back to the dot it started drawing from. The classic example is the 5-pointed golden star, where you move 2 dots while drawing. After render you can choose to show more details about which stars can be drawn given that amount of dots. For more mathematical details, search on the Internet for GCD (Greatest Common Divisor).

The Mandelbrot set is the set of complex numbers c for which the function f(z) = z² + c does not diverge to infinity when iterated from z = 0. It is one of the most famous examples of fractal geometry. \n\nUse pinch-to-zoom to explore the infinite boundaries of the set!
This hypotrochoid is traced by a wheel of radius %1$d rolling inside a ring of radius %2$d, with the pen %3$d from the wheel centre.
This epitrochoid is traced by a wheel of radius %1$d rolling around the outside of a ring of radius %2$d, with the pen %3$d from the wheel centre.
The curve closes after %1$d turns of the wheel, because gcd(%2$d, %3$d) = %4$d.
It has %1$d lobes, the fixed ring divided by that gcd.
The pen sits on the wheel rim, so this is a hypocycloid, a special hypotrochoid with sharp cusps.
The pen sits on the wheel rim, so this is an epicycloid, a special epitrochoid with sharp cusps.
The pen is at the wheel centre, so the trace is a circle.

A Spirograph traces the path of a pen attached to a circle rolling around a fixed circle, the same idea as the toothed rings and wheels in the toy.

When the two radii are whole numbers, the curve eventually closes. The number of loops is governed by the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the two radii, the same arithmetic that decides which star figures can be drawn in one stroke.

Drag the sliders to change the ring, the wheel, and how far the pen sits from the wheel centre. Switch off roll-inside to roll on the outside instead (an epitrochoid).
Spirograph with fixed ring %1$d, rolling wheel %2$d, pen distance %3$d. Pinch to zoom, drag to pan, double tap to zoom in.
The critical point z = 0 stays bounded, so this Julia set is connected. Its c sits inside the Mandelbrot set.
The critical point z = 0 escapes, so this Julia set is a cloud of dust. Its c sits outside the Mandelbrot set.

This Julia set is generated by iterating z → z² + c from each point in the complex plane, with c held fixed at %1$s (%2$s).

%3$s

The Mandelbrot set answers which values of c produce a connected Julia set. This screen answers what a single c looks like.

Use the slider to try well-known values of c. Pinch to zoom and drag to pan through the fractal.
Star drawing with %1$d dots, moving %2$d at a time. Pinch to zoom, drag to pan, double tap to zoom in.
Mandelbrot set. Pinch to zoom, drag to pan, double tap to zoom in.
Julia set. Pinch to zoom, drag to pan, double tap to zoom in. Use the slider to change c.
